turbovec and vector evolution: Local Search Faster than the FAISS

The video explains turbovec, a Rust vector index with Python interface based on the TurboQuant algorithm. It shows why memory is the bottleneck of vector search in RAG, how FAISS bypasses this with product quantization and FastScan, and how TurboQuant compresses vectors without training phase, near the theoretical limit.

The memory bottle

Who builds RAG applications (increased generation by recovery) knows that large-scale vector search becomes an engineering challenge as data grows 00:00.

The account that the video uses: 10 million uncompressed documents occupy about 31 GB of RAM in float32 format 00:22. With the right optimization, the same corpus drops to about 4 GB, which makes local architectures viable 00:43.

The script goes through memory bottleneck, FAISS compression with FastScan, TurboQuant, algorithm operation and turbovec 00:43.

When climbing AI applications, sooner or later you hit the memory wall. Reading without stopping large vectors in direct float32 from RAM locks the CPU, and so the industry sought aggressive compression 01:03.

FAISS, Product Quantization and FastScan

The most common solution is the Facebook FAISS library. The basis is product quantization (PQ): break each vector into subvectors and exchange each part for a short code, which points to a code book, the query table 01:46.

The problem is latency. With the tables in RAM, the search gets slow, because the CPU calculates much faster than it accesses the memory 02:08.

FAISS FastScan solves this by taking RAM tables to CPU SIMD loggers, which are much faster. It packs 4-bit codes into 32-byte blocks 02:30.

The Advance of TurboQuant

To overcome FAISS without losing precision, researchers resorted to theoretical mathematics 02:52.

A milestone was the article by RaBitQ, by SIGMOD 2024, which showed that it was possible to have a strict theoretical error limit with random quantization 03:13.

TurboQuant emerged on that basis. According to the video, it will be presented at ICLR 2026 03:13. The article states that the algorithm is at a factor of about 2.7 of the lower theoretical limit of compression 03:34.

The great practical advantage: the classic PQ requires a training of grouping with k-means to assemble the code book. TurboQuant is data independent and has no training phase; you can add vectors without rebuilding tables 03:54.

How the algorithm works

The pipeline has five steps that transform large vectors into compact codes, maintaining accuracy 04:15:

1. Normalization: Vectors have seen unitary directions in a hypersphere 04:35. 2. Random rotation: force each coordinate following a predictable distribution, Beta distribution 04:35. 3. Calibration: fine tuning in smaller dimensions 04:35. 4. Lloyd-Max: The algorithm calculates the best quantization intervals 04:57. 5. Packaging: everything turns whole 2 or 4 bits 04:57.

Compression usually underestimates the distances between vectors. With an adapted idea from RaBitQ, the system holds an extra scalar per vector, which eliminates this bias of the internal product almost without cost 04:57.

Turbovec in practice

Turbovec takes TurboQuant to code, written in Rust 05:19. According to the video, with kernels optimized by hand for NEON, it can be 12% to 20% faster than FAISS FastScan on ARM chips 05:39. The project page, read in 11/19/2026, shows larger numbers: about 4 times 4 bits and 2 times 2 bits against IndexPQFastScan, with 100,000 vectors, in ARM and x86.

Another point is filtering. In a common search, the data comes to memory and only then are filtered and discarded 06:00. Turbovec filters inside the SIMD register: not allowed vectors are ignored before scoring 06:00.

Integration is simple: there are connectors for LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack and Agno. Just change the import at the top of the code, and the rest of the pipeline remains the same 06:22.

The limit of local machines

The video leaves a question: if 31 GB fits in 4 GB with fast search, what is the limit of local machines? For many teams, dependence on expensive vector banks in the cloud may cease to exist 06:43.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does turbovec need to train the index before use?

Nope. TurboQuant is data independent and has no training phase; vectors enter continuously 03:54.

How much memory does turbovec save?

In the video example, 10 million documents fall from about 31 GB in float32 to about 4 GB 00:43.

Fonts

  • RyanCodrai/turbovec (GitHub)Project Repository: a TurboQuant-based vector index written in Rust with bindings for Python, MIT license. Claims that 10 million 768-dimensional embeddings occupy 31 GB in float32 and about 4 GB in turbovec; uses 2 or 4 bits per dimension; has no training step; filters by list of IDs or mask; and integrates LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack and Agno.
  • TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion RateAn article by Zandieh, Daliri, Hadian and Mirrokni (arXiv, April 2025). It describes an independent quantizer for online use, which rotates the vectors randomly to induce a Beta distribution at the coordinates and is at a factor of about 2.7 of the lower theoretical limit.
  • RaBitQ: Quantizing High-Dimensional Vectors with a theoretical error Bound for approximate Nearest Neighbor SearchArticle Gao and Long, accepted in SIGMOD 2024. It proposes a random quantization with theoretical error limit, in contrast to product quantization, which does not have this limit.

Reviewed by Maurício Yokoyama Issei in 19 November 2026.

About the video

In this video, we explore turbovec, a high performance vector index written in Rust with bindings for Python that is transforming the creation of local and private RAG systems
.
Learn how turbovec uses the TurboQuant algorithm (of Google Research) to perform impressive achievements: compress a corpus of 10 million documents into just 4 GB of RAM and perform faster searches than the market standard, FAISS
. All this without data training phase (totally online management) and maintaining high accuracy
.
In the video, we address the technical innovations that make this possible, including TQ+ coordinate calibration, Lloyd-Max scalar quantization and extreme optimization using SIMD hardware instructions (NEON for ARM and AVX-512BW for x86)
. If you build RAG architectures and worry about data privacy, memory consumption or low latency, this technology is for you!
.
